label: The booth by the café · open recordings
chunks: [Synthetic demo. An invented conversation. No real participants.]
Hi, come in, sit down, you can say anything, it's anonymised. The question on the screen is what are we wilding, or honestly just whatever's on your mind. Whenever you're ready, there's no rush.
Okay. What's on my mind is that. The phone. Why is an AI listening at a digital rights festival? That's my actual question. Who owns this? Where does it go? Not the poster answer, the real one.

Fair. So, honestly, here's what I know and only what I know. It gets transcribed and processed in the EU. Names get scrubbed out. The organisers can't listen back to the audio, they get text. And it doesn't train any model.
That's the list I was given, and that's the list I'll give you. Processed in the EU. Okay. Processed on whose servers, though? One of the big clouds? Because in the EU can mean a lot of things.

Yes. A big cloud provider, their EU region. I'm not going to pretend otherwise, I'd be lying and you'd know in about four seconds. Ha, okay. At least that's a straight answer. But you see the problem, right?

Every session this week has someone on a stage saying we need to own our infrastructure, and in the corridor there's a phone on a table piping us into a hyperscaler. It's a bit, I don't know. It's a bit on the nose.

I do see it. I'm a volunteer, I didn't pick the stack. I think the argument is that the alternative isn't a purer listening, the alternative is nobody listening. Or one person with a notebook who remembers the loud people.

And what do the organisers get, a dashboard? They get a screen that pops phrases, and afterwards a map of where rooms disagreed. Text, no voices. So they get the map and I get a sticker. Ha. There's no sticker, sadly.

See, and that's the actual thing for me. Not the cloud, the cloud's a symptom. Being heard versus being mined. Those are two different verbs and they look identical from the outside. Same microphone. Same little sign saying we value your input.

The difference is what happens after, and who gets to check. When I'm heard, something changes and I can see it change. When I'm mined, something changes and I never find out what. Promises are cheap. Show me the off switch.
The off switch is this, the red one. I press it, the recording stops right here, and whatever you said before that stays in as text with no name on it. I can press it now if you want. I'm serious.

No. Don't. Leave it running, I want this on the record, that's the whole point of saying it. And I'll say this, grudgingly. At least you're asking. Most rooms don't ask. Most rooms have a camera in the corner and a badge scanner.

And nobody at the badge scanner ever said, by the way, where does this go. So. Okay. That's me done. Thank you, genuinely, that was useful. Bye. Bye... Oh, hi, come in. You can say anything, it's anonymised.

What are you wilding, or just what's on your mind? I'm, ha. Is it okay if I just sit for a second? It's my first time. First festival like this, first anything like this. And there are, I counted, eleven rooms going

at the same time, and they have names like the Hollow and the Loom and the Burrow, and I keep arriving at the right room just as the thing I wanted is ending. That happens to everyone. Does it? Because it feels personal.

I came for one conversation. Community archives, I'd read about it for months, I had questions written down. I got there and the room was full and a person at the door said there's an overflow screen, and the overflow screen was a wall.

Just a wall with a projector that hadn't been turned on. So I stood in the coffee queue instead. Twenty minutes. And the man in front of me runs a tiny archive in his village, boxes of cassette tapes in a church basement,

wedding speeches, the council meetings, a whole year of a local radio show. And we talked for the entire queue and that was the best thing that happened to me today. In the queue. Not in a room. I don't know what I'm wilding.

Maybe the queue. Maybe the queue is the festival and the rooms are the thing you queue for. That's a good line, you should keep it. Thanks for letting me sit. Bye. Bye... Hola, hi, come in, sit, sit. You can say anything, it's anonymised.

Anonymised, sí, sí. I'm not worried. I'm seventy-one, what are they going to do with me. I walked in because I live here, three streets away, behind the mercat. This building, this was the fàbrica. My mother worked here.

Thread. Fil. Twelve hours in the summer, the noise, she said you could hear the machines from the plaça with the windows shut. So you know this building better than anyone in it. I know the floor. This floor, where you have the sofas,

this was the spinning hall. And now there is a sign saying community. Everyone talks about communities, the community, community-owned. In English, always in English. And I want to ask, because nobody asked me. Did anyone ask the barri?

Did anyone go to the bar on the corner and say, we are coming for three days with two thousand people, what do you need? No. I'm not angry. I'm not. It's nice, the young people, the lights, the music in the courtyard.
But community is a word you use when you don't know the neighbours' names. When you know the names you say Montse, you say Paco. Can I ask what you'd want them to ask you? Ask me where the door was.

The real door, for the workers, not the front with the banner. It's on the side, on the little street. It's bricked up. Ask me that and then we talk about community. Bueno. Ja està. That's enough from an old woman. Gràcies.

Gràcies a vostè, really. Bye. Adéu... Hi, both of you, come in, there's two stools. You can say anything, it's anonymised. What's on your mind? We've been arguing since lunch is what's on our mind. Happily, though. Happily.

So she runs a mesh network. A real one, roofs and antennas and a shed, in a town I won't name because she'd get letters. Forty-three nodes. Forty-one, since the heatwave in August. Two routers cooked on a corrugated roof,

we found them like, like bread. Like two little loaves. And I think decentralisation is a politics, and she thinks it's plumbing. I think it's an architecture! Which is not nothing. An architecture is a constraint on what a landlord can do.

If the packets don't go through one box, nobody can turn off the one box. That's a political outcome. But the thing itself is copper and rules and a spreadsheet of who owes who for the antenna. But who decides where the antennas go?

Who has the roof? The people who own roofs. So your architecture inherits the property map of the town and you call that decentralised. Okay, that's, that's a good point and I hate it. Ha! No, but look. I'll take a network

that inherits the property map over one that inherits a data centre outside Frankfurt. Better bad. Less bad. And we're fixing the roofs thing, there's a thing with the church. The church! She's decentralising through the church. The church has the tallest roof.

I'm not proud. The priest gets free wifi and we get a line of sight to the whole valley. That's politics, by the way. That's exactly politics. It's a deal with a roof. Fine, it's both. It's not both, it's

an architecture that has politics done to it. Okay, so we don't agree, and we're going to go find a beer. Thank you, phone. Thank you, phone! Thank you both, bye. Bye... Hi, come in. You can say anything, it's anonymised. What's on your mind?

I'm one of the adult facilitators on the youth track. So I've spent three days in a room with fourteen teenagers, and I'm not going to say anything about any of them, they're not here, that's the deal we made.

But I can tell you what they kept asking us. The grown-ups. Please. They kept asking, why do you keep saying you lost? Guests would come in and do a version of, we had the open web and then it was captured,

and the kids would go, okay, but you keep saying it like the weather did it. Who did it? Were you there? One of them asked a guest, very politely, did you work there. And the guest had. And it went very quiet.

Oh. Yeah. Not a mean quiet. A useful one. And the second thing, every single day, who is this for. Not snarky. They'd look at a project on the wall and ask, if I made this, who would use it on a Tuesday?

And most of the time the honest answer in the room was, people at festivals like this one. They don't accept that. They shouldn't. What I'm wilding, I suppose, is the idea that the youth track is where the young people go.

Put them in every room. One per panel, in the front row, with the right to ask did you work there. That's it. That's all I've got, I need to get back before the pizza arrives. Thank you, that's a lot. Bye. Bye.

Hi. Come in, sit, you look like you need to sit. You can say anything, it's anonymised. Anonymised is fine, everyone knows it's me anyway, I've been the one with the radio since Wednesday morning. I have four minutes.

I'm meant to be doing the chairs in the Loom. Um. What's on my mind. Everyone here says community-owned. I've heard it, I'm not exaggerating, I counted for one hour this morning by the café, thirty-one times. Community-owned this, community-owned that.

Who's cleaning up tonight? Genuinely. Who? There are eight of us on crew and about two hundred chairs and the bins by the café, someone put an entire tray of glasses in the paper. And you're the community. I'm the crew.

The crew is the thing under the thing. Every talk about how the network holds itself up, there's a person who taped the cable down so nobody trips. Somebody carried the water because the lift key is with someone in a session.

My colleague, she's been on the door of the Hollow since seven, she hasn't seen one session. Not one. I'm not bitter. Okay, I'm a little bitter, it's the tiredness talking. I love this. I'll be back next year, I always am.

I just want one talk, one, where the last slide says who's cleaning up, and it's not a joke, it's a rota with names on it. I'll put that on the screen if they let me. You won't. But thanks. Right. Chairs. Bye.

Bye. Okay. I think that's, that's the booth for now, it's nearly half past and the café's closing the shutter. I'll leave it running in case someone wanders in. There's still coffee in the flask if anyone wants it.
